screens.title: Scene Management and Basic Asset Import
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn practical scene management and the basics of importing assets into Unity. A scene is a self-contained part of your game — a main menu, a level, or a cinematic — and using separate scenes helps you load only what's necessary and keep memory usage manageable. You'll practice creating, saving, and switching scenes, then build a clean Project window structure with folders like _Scenes, _Models, _Textures, and _Audio so assets are easy to find and reuse. We also cover importing common file types and the Inspector import settings you should review: model scale and materials, texture type and compression, and audio load type. As you follow along, notice the practical trade-offs: higher texture quality improves fidelity but increases build size; aggressive compression reduces size but can introduce artifacts. A simple habit — placing scenes in a dedicated _Scenes folder and checking import settings immediately after import — prevents many headaches later. By the end you'll be able to set up scenes and import assets with confidence, understand why each import setting matters, and avoid the common mistakes that create clutter or poor performance. Which asset will you adjust first when optimizing a scene's load time?

screens.title: What is a Scene in Unity?
screens.narratorSegment: A scene in Unity is a self-contained container that includes GameObjects, lighting, cameras, and environment settings which together form a distinct part of your game such as a level, a menu, or a cinematic. Think of each scene as a stage: it holds the actors, the props, and the lighting for that moment in the game. Using multiple scenes separates responsibilities — your main menu doesn't need to load level geometry, and a loading screen can exist alone to minimize memory use. This modular approach improves performance because Unity only loads assets for active scenes into memory, and it simplifies collaboration since different team members can work on separate scenes concurrently. A common misconception is that everything must be in a single scene for easier reference; in practice that creates huge files, slower save times, and harder asset tracking. For example, save your MainMenu scene and Level01 scene separately, then open each to test specific behavior. Also know that Unity allows multi-scene editing for advanced use, but by default only one scene is active for play and editing. Key takeaway: use separate scenes for distinct game sections, save them in a dedicated _Scenes folder, and develop a habit of frequent saves to prevent data loss. Which part of your current project would benefit most from being moved into its own scene?

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › What is a Scene?
Definition

Scene

A container for GameObjects, lighting, cameras, and environment settings representing a specific part of your game.

Metaphor: Stage
Actors, props, and lighting on a stage correspond to GameObjects, assets, and scene settings.
Common mistake
Keeping everything in one large scene causes slow saves, large memory use, and team conflicts.
Key Takeaway

Use separate scenes for distinct gameplay sections and save them in a dedicated _Scenes folder.

Concrete example
Example: MainMenu and Level01
Save MainMenu.scene hosting UI elements and Level01.scene hosting gameplay objects. Load only the scene you need to reduce memory usage.
Check your understanding
  • Why does separating scenes help with performance?
  • When might multi-scene editing be useful?
Misconception: splitting scenes harms performance — in fact it lets you control what loads and therefore helps performance.

screens.title: Create, Save, and Open Scenes
screens.narratorSegment: Follow a consistent process when creating and saving scenes to avoid data loss and to maintain clarity in your project. Start by creating a dedicated folder named _Scenes in the Project window. Then use File → New Scene to start a fresh scene. If Unity prompts to save changes in the current scene, do not ignore it — always save the current scene first. Use File → Save Scene or the shortcut to save quickly. When naming scenes, choose clear names like MainMenu and Level01 so they are self-explanatory. Save them inside the _Scenes folder you created. To open a scene later, double-click the scene asset in the Project window or use File → Open Scene. You can also drag a scene into the Hierarchy to load it. Remember that Unity defaults to a single active scene for editing and play; multi-scene editing exists but is an advanced workflow. A common error is forgetting to save before creating a new scene and losing unsaved changes. Another is scattering scene files across many folders — this makes them hard to find. Practice the sequence: create folder, new scene, save as MainMenu, new scene, save as Level01, open each to verify. This habit reduces friction and ensures your scenes are discoverable and safe.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Create, Save, Open
Process Flow

Create, save, and open scenes

  1. Create folder: right-click Assets → Create → Folder, name it _Scenes.
  2. New scene: File → New Scene. Unity may prompt to save current changes — save them.
  3. Save: File → Save Scene or Ctrl+S. Name scene MainMenu and place it in _Scenes.
  4. Create another: File → New Scene, Save as Level01 into _Scenes.
  5. Open scene: double-click scene asset or drag into Hierarchy to load.
Common mistake
Not saving before creating a new scene leads to lost changes.
Example workflow
Create _Scenes, save MainMenu, open MainMenu, add UI, save. Create Level01, save, add test cube, open Level01 to verify.
Key Takeaway

A consistent save and naming process prevents lost work and makes scenes easy to find.

screens.title: Project Window and Folder Structure
screens.narratorSegment: The Project window is the central place where all of your project's assets live: models, textures, audio, scripts, materials, prefabs, and animations. Without a clear folder structure, assets accumulate and make the project hard to navigate, which slows development and complicates team collaboration. Adopt a simple convention early: create top-level folders such as _Scenes, _Scripts, _Models, _Textures, _Materials, _Audio, _Prefabs, and _Animations. The underscore prefix helps these folders climb to the top of the alphabetical list in the Project window, so important folders stay visible. When you import new assets, immediately move them to the appropriate folder and rename them sensibly so others understand their purpose. For example, place a player model under _Models/Player and its face texture under _Textures/Player. A typical mistake is creating many nested, inconsistent folders that mirror a designer's local system — this hurts portability and discoverability. Keep folder depth reasonable, use consistent casing and prefixes, and document the structure in a small README asset if you're working with a team. After establishing the structure, build a simple habit: import, then move, then inspect import settings. That three-step routine keeps the Project window tidy and predictable.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Project Window
Architecture

Folder structure that scales

Use top-level folders with underscore prefixes and consistent naming to make assets discoverable and portable across machines.

Recommended top-level folders
_Scenes, _Scripts, _Models, _Textures, _Materials, _Audio, _Prefabs, _Animations
Team tip
Add a small text README in the Assets root to document naming conventions for your team.
Concrete example
A player character: put the model at _Models/Player/hero.fbx, textures at _Textures/Player/face.png, and animations at _Animations/Player/walk.anim. This keeps all player-related files grouped but still searchable at the top level.
Common mistake

Scattering files across many nested folders or keeping raw local paths makes it hard for others to find assets.

Why it matters: a clear structure speeds development, reduces merge conflicts, and simplifies asset reuse.

screens.title: Importing Assets — Drag & Drop Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Importing assets in Unity is simple: drag files from your operating system into the desired folder inside the Project window. Common file types include. fbx,. obj, and. blend for 3D models;. png,. jpg,. tga, and. psd for textures; and. wav or. mp3 for audio. After drop-in, Unity scans and processes the file and creates an internal asset representation. The first thing to do is select the new asset and inspect its Import Settings in the Inspector window. For a model, check the scale factor and material import options. For a texture, verify the texture type and compression. For audio, verify load type and compression format. A reliable workflow is: create or select target folder (for example _Models), drag the file into it, select the asset, then immediately open the Inspector to confirm defaults. This avoids the common mistake of leaving assets in the root folder or never tuning their settings. If the model uses external materials or textures, ensure those textures are imported and linked correctly. Finally, test the imported asset by dragging it into an empty scene to validate scale and appearance. This immediate test prevents surprises during level assembly.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Import: Drag & Drop
Process

Drag, inspect, and test

  1. Create or select the target folder, e.g., _Models.
  2. Drag the model or texture file from the OS into the Project window.
  3. Select the imported asset and open the Inspector to review import settings.
  4. Drag the asset into a test scene to verify scale, material links, and appearance.
Quick tip
Move new imports into the correct folder immediately to keep the Project window tidy.
Example
Drag hero.fbx into _Models, hero_diffuse.png into _Textures, then select hero.fbx and check its Scale Factor in the Inspector. If it appears too large or small in the test scene, adjust scale and reapply.
Key Takeaway

Importing is fast, but inspecting settings and testing the asset prevents later surprises.

screens.title: Model Import Settings
screens.narratorSegment: When you import a 3D model, Unity provides import settings that control how the model appears and behaves in your scene. The Scale Factor determines how the model's units map to Unity units; change this if the model is too small or too large compared with other objects. Material import options let Unity create or link materials; if you prefer custom materials, disable automatic material creation and assign them manually. If the model contains animations, you can choose to import them and configure clips, loop behavior, and root motion. Always inspect the mesh compression and normals settings: incorrect normals can cause lighting artifacts, while aggressive mesh compression can reduce fidelity. A common misconception is to trust default import options for all models; while defaults are convenient, they may be inappropriate for key characters or assets that must meet strict visual fidelity. A concrete example: import a character model that appears twice the expected size; adjust the Scale Factor from 1 to 0.5, apply, and retest in a scene with a 1-meter cube to verify scale. After changes, consider creating a prefab for repeated use so you don't repeat the same adjustments manually. Which model setting will you check first when importing a character?

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Model Import
Model Import Settings
Key controls: Scale Factor, Materials, Animation Clips, Normals & Tangents, Mesh Compression.
Scale Factor
Adjust to match Unity units. Test with a reference cube to confirm.
Material Import
Auto-created materials save time but may require cleanup for consistent shading.
Animations
Import available clips and configure loop and root motion options.
Concrete example
A downloaded character appears oversized. Set Scale Factor to 0.5, apply, then place next to a 1-meter cube to confirm visual scale and collision alignment.
Misconception

Default import options are always sufficient — often not true for character models requiring precise scale and animation settings.

screens.title: Texture Import Settings
screens.narratorSegment: Texture import settings directly affect visual fidelity and build size. The main controls are Texture Type — for example Default for general textures, Normal Map for bump maps, and Sprite for 2D UI and sprites — and Compression, which reduces file size but may introduce visible artifacts. For UI icons or small sprites, higher compression is usually acceptable because they display at small sizes. For a character's face texture, choose lower compression or higher quality to preserve detail. Mipmaps and filter mode also matter: enable mipmaps for textures visible at multiple distances to improve filtering and reduce shimmering. A common mistake is importing all textures at maximum resolution and no compression; that bloats builds. Another mistake is over-compressing important textures and losing sharp detail. For a practical approach, categorize textures by use: UI icons (high compression), environment tiling textures (medium compression, mipmaps), character albedos (lower compression). After changing compression, inspect the compressed preview in the Inspector and test in a scene to ensure acceptable quality. The key decision is always use-case-driven: choose the setting that gives acceptable quality at the smallest size for that purpose.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Texture Import Settings
Comparison

Quality vs Size

UI Icons
Use higher compression and smaller resolutions; artifacts are less noticeable at small sizes.
Character Textures
Prefer lower compression and keep higher resolution for faces and key details.
Environment Textures
Use mipmaps and medium compression to maintain quality across distances.
Concrete example
A high-resolution terrain albedo should have mipmaps enabled and medium compression; a small UI icon can use aggressive compression to save size without visible loss.
Key Takeaway

Choose texture type and compression based on intended on-screen size and importance to visual fidelity.

screens.title: Audio Import Settings
screens.narratorSegment: Audio import settings control memory footprint and playback behavior. Key options include Load Type — such as Decompress On Load, Compressed In Memory, or Streaming — and compression format and quality. Use Decompress On Load for very short sounds that must play with minimal latency, but remember they will occupy memory equal to their uncompressed size. Use Compressed In Memory for moderate-length clips where you need lower memory use but slightly more C P U cost to decompress. Use Streaming for long music tracks or cutscenes to avoid loading large audio files entirely into memory. Another important setting is sample rate conversion and quality: reducing sample rate reduces size but can cost fidelity. A common mistake is importing long music tracks with Decompress On Load, which can massively increase memory. For game UI sounds, prefer compressed formats and keep clips short. For an example, import a 90-second background music as Streaming and an interface click sound as Compressed In Memory; test that playback is reliable and latency acceptable. The main decision is based on length and performance needs: stream long content, keep short sounds quickly accessible, and adjust quality to balance size and audio clarity.

Definition

Audio Import Settings

  • Load Type: Decompress On Load, Compressed In Memory, Streaming.
  • Compression Format & Quality: adjust to balance clarity and size.
  • Sample Rate: reduce for savings when high fidelity is unnecessary.
Concrete example
Use Streaming for a 90-second background track to avoid loading it fully into memory. Use Compressed In Memory for short UI clicks to reduce size while keeping latency low.
Common mistake

Importing long music as Decompress On Load greatly increases memory and can harm performance.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Two recurring mistakes derail small and large Unity projects alike: poor organization and ignoring import settings. Poor organization manifests as assets dumped into the Assets root or inconsistent naming — this makes finding files slow and increases the chance of duplicate imports. Ignoring import settings leads to oversized builds or visual artifacts. To avoid these issues adopt three simple best practices: first, create and enforce a top-level folder convention at project start, using underscore prefixes for the most important folders; second, make a habit of inspecting import settings immediately after import and document decisions; third, create prefabs or shared materials for reused assets so changes propagate rather than requiring repeated edits. Additionally, include a short README in your Assets root describing folder rules so all contributors follow the same pattern. When troubleshooting performance problems, check textures and audio first: they often explain sudden increases in build size or memory usage. A final note: small, consistent habits prevent large cleanup efforts later — the time to organize and inspect is now, not after the project becomes unwieldy. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn practical scene management and the basics of importing assets into Unity. A scene is a self-contained part of your game — a main menu, a level, or a cinematic — and using separate scenes helps you load only what's necessary and keep memory usage manageable. You'll practice creating, saving, and switching scenes, then build a clean Project window structure with folders like _Scenes, _Models, _Textures, and _Audio so assets are easy to find and reuse. We also cover importing common file types and the Inspector import settings you should review: model scale and materials, texture type and compression, and audio load type. As you follow along, notice the practical trade-offs: higher texture quality improves fidelity but increases build size; aggressive compression reduces size but can introduce artifacts. A simple habit — placing scenes in a dedicated _Scenes folder and checking import settings immediately after import — prevents many headaches later. By the end you'll be able to set up scenes and import assets with confidence, understand why each import setting matters, and avoid the common mistakes that create clutter or poor performance. Which asset will you adjust first when optimizing a scene's load time?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to create and manage multiple scenes, build a clear folder structure in the Project window, import common asset types, and adjust import settings to control performance and file size. First, you'll learn to create, save, and open scenes reliably so you never lose work and can separate gameplay areas. Second, you will organize assets into top-level folders with a naming convention that surfaces important directories to the top of the Project window. Third, you'll import 3D models, textures, and audio using drag-and-drop and recognize file formats Unity accepts. Finally, you will inspect and modify key import settings such as model scale, texture compression, and audio load type, knowing which changes reduce memory use and which preserve visual fidelity. Each objective here has a short practical task and a milestone: create _Scenes and save two example scenes; create _Models and _Textures and import a sample model and texture; open import settings and change scale or compression; and run a simple check on build size. These skills matter because they prevent chaotic projects, reduce commit conflicts, and make it straightforward to optimize a game's performance. Consider which objective will give you the biggest immediate payoff in your current project.

This slide turns the objectives into hands-on milestones you can complete quickly. For creating and saving scenes, your milestone is to make a _Scenes folder and save a MainMenu and Level01 scene inside it, then reopen each scene to ensure they load. For asset organization, create top-level folders named _Models, _Textures, _Audio, _Materials and move any sample files into the right folders. For importing assets, drag a model file and a texture file into the appropriate folders and confirm they appear in the Project window. For import settings, open the Inspector for the imported model and change the scale factor, and open the texture settings and change compression; observe the preview and any warnings. These small tasks demonstrate practical competence: you should be able to repeat them consistently and explain why each step matters. The milestones are intentionally short so you can integrate them into a normal workflow and prevent the common mistake of leaving assets unreviewed. After completing them, you will have concrete evidence that your scenes load correctly and that your assets import with sensible defaults you can adjust. Which milestone will you complete first in your current project?

A scene in Unity is a self-contained container that includes GameObjects, lighting, cameras, and environment settings which together form a distinct part of your game such as a level, a menu, or a cinematic. Think of each scene as a stage: it holds the actors, the props, and the lighting for that moment in the game. Using multiple scenes separates responsibilities — your main menu doesn't need to load level geometry, and a loading screen can exist alone to minimize memory use. This modular approach improves performance because Unity only loads assets for active scenes into memory, and it simplifies collaboration since different team members can work on separate scenes concurrently. A common misconception is that everything must be in a single scene for easier reference; in practice that creates huge files, slower save times, and harder asset tracking. For example, save your MainMenu scene and Level01 scene separately, then open each to test specific behavior. Also know that Unity allows multi-scene editing for advanced use, but by default only one scene is active for play and editing. Key takeaway: use separate scenes for distinct game sections, save them in a dedicated _Scenes folder, and develop a habit of frequent saves to prevent data loss. Which part of your current project would benefit most from being moved into its own scene?

Follow a consistent process when creating and saving scenes to avoid data loss and to maintain clarity in your project. Start by creating a dedicated folder named _Scenes in the Project window. Then use File → New Scene to start a fresh scene. If Unity prompts to save changes in the current scene, do not ignore it — always save the current scene first. Use File → Save Scene or the shortcut to save quickly. When naming scenes, choose clear names like MainMenu and Level01 so they are self-explanatory. Save them inside the _Scenes folder you created. To open a scene later, double-click the scene asset in the Project window or use File → Open Scene. You can also drag a scene into the Hierarchy to load it. Remember that Unity defaults to a single active scene for editing and play; multi-scene editing exists but is an advanced workflow. A common error is forgetting to save before creating a new scene and losing unsaved changes. Another is scattering scene files across many folders — this makes them hard to find. Practice the sequence: create folder, new scene, save as MainMenu, new scene, save as Level01, open each to verify. This habit reduces friction and ensures your scenes are discoverable and safe.

The Project window is the central place where all of your project's assets live: models, textures, audio, scripts, materials, prefabs, and animations. Without a clear folder structure, assets accumulate and make the project hard to navigate, which slows development and complicates team collaboration. Adopt a simple convention early: create top-level folders such as _Scenes, _Scripts, _Models, _Textures, _Materials, _Audio, _Prefabs, and _Animations. The underscore prefix helps these folders climb to the top of the alphabetical list in the Project window, so important folders stay visible. When you import new assets, immediately move them to the appropriate folder and rename them sensibly so others understand their purpose. For example, place a player model under _Models/Player and its face texture under _Textures/Player. A typical mistake is creating many nested, inconsistent folders that mirror a designer's local system — this hurts portability and discoverability. Keep folder depth reasonable, use consistent casing and prefixes, and document the structure in a small README asset if you're working with a team. After establishing the structure, build a simple habit: import, then move, then inspect import settings. That three-step routine keeps the Project window tidy and predictable.

Importing assets in Unity is simple: drag files from your operating system into the desired folder inside the Project window. Common file types include. fbx,. obj, and. blend for 3D models;. png,. jpg,. tga, and. psd for textures; and. wav or. mp3 for audio. After drop-in, Unity scans and processes the file and creates an internal asset representation. The first thing to do is select the new asset and inspect its Import Settings in the Inspector window. For a model, check the scale factor and material import options. For a texture, verify the texture type and compression. For audio, verify load type and compression format. A reliable workflow is: create or select target folder (for example _Models), drag the file into it, select the asset, then immediately open the Inspector to confirm defaults. This avoids the common mistake of leaving assets in the root folder or never tuning their settings. If the model uses external materials or textures, ensure those textures are imported and linked correctly. Finally, test the imported asset by dragging it into an empty scene to validate scale and appearance. This immediate test prevents surprises during level assembly.

When you import a 3D model, Unity provides import settings that control how the model appears and behaves in your scene. The Scale Factor determines how the model's units map to Unity units; change this if the model is too small or too large compared with other objects. Material import options let Unity create or link materials; if you prefer custom materials, disable automatic material creation and assign them manually. If the model contains animations, you can choose to import them and configure clips, loop behavior, and root motion. Always inspect the mesh compression and normals settings: incorrect normals can cause lighting artifacts, while aggressive mesh compression can reduce fidelity. A common misconception is to trust default import options for all models; while defaults are convenient, they may be inappropriate for key characters or assets that must meet strict visual fidelity. A concrete example: import a character model that appears twice the expected size; adjust the Scale Factor from 1 to 0.5, apply, and retest in a scene with a 1-meter cube to verify scale. After changes, consider creating a prefab for repeated use so you don't repeat the same adjustments manually. Which model setting will you check first when importing a character?

Texture import settings directly affect visual fidelity and build size. The main controls are Texture Type — for example Default for general textures, Normal Map for bump maps, and Sprite for 2D UI and sprites — and Compression, which reduces file size but may introduce visible artifacts. For UI icons or small sprites, higher compression is usually acceptable because they display at small sizes. For a character's face texture, choose lower compression or higher quality to preserve detail. Mipmaps and filter mode also matter: enable mipmaps for textures visible at multiple distances to improve filtering and reduce shimmering. A common mistake is importing all textures at maximum resolution and no compression; that bloats builds. Another mistake is over-compressing important textures and losing sharp detail. For a practical approach, categorize textures by use: UI icons (high compression), environment tiling textures (medium compression, mipmaps), character albedos (lower compression). After changing compression, inspect the compressed preview in the Inspector and test in a scene to ensure acceptable quality. The key decision is always use-case-driven: choose the setting that gives acceptable quality at the smallest size for that purpose.

Audio import settings control memory footprint and playback behavior. Key options include Load Type — such as Decompress On Load, Compressed In Memory, or Streaming — and compression format and quality. Use Decompress On Load for very short sounds that must play with minimal latency, but remember they will occupy memory equal to their uncompressed size. Use Compressed In Memory for moderate-length clips where you need lower memory use but slightly more C P U cost to decompress. Use Streaming for long music tracks or cutscenes to avoid loading large audio files entirely into memory. Another important setting is sample rate conversion and quality: reducing sample rate reduces size but can cost fidelity. A common mistake is importing long music tracks with Decompress On Load, which can massively increase memory. For game UI sounds, prefer compressed formats and keep clips short. For an example, import a 90-second background music as Streaming and an interface click sound as Compressed In Memory; test that playback is reliable and latency acceptable. The main decision is based on length and performance needs: stream long content, keep short sounds quickly accessible, and adjust quality to balance size and audio clarity.
